extraction_limitations: The LiteratureAtom schema is oriented toward primary literature and has no dedicated secondary-reported-result kind. Qualitative review summaries use existing atom kinds plus secondary_reported_result tags.
The review does not report a PRISMA-style flow, duplicate screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment, evidence grading, or quantitative meta-analysis.
The extraction preserves major review-level assertions and selected study-level examples rather than atomizing every statement about all 246 cited references.
All atoms remain needs_review because no independent human verification step is represented.
No external web verification was performed because @VERIFY was not activated.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to discuss bromelain's biological effects on human health, medical and food-industry uses, and future prospects using the available literature.
The authors searched PubMed using bromelain alone and combined with cancer, inflammation, cardiovascular diseases, coagulation, fibrinolysis, medicine, and SARS-CoV-2 virus.
Eligible articles were published before 1 October 2021.
Eligible articles were written in English.
The authors screened relevance by title and abstract, then evaluated full text for articles meeting the search criteria.
The review reported no external funding.
The authors declared no conflict of interest.
The article stated that data sharing was not applicable.
The review reports that commercial bromelain extract is approximately 80% stem bromelain, 10% fruit bromelain, 5% ananain, with other components making up the remainder.
Stem bromelain and fruit bromelain differ in biological activity, structure, and physicochemical properties.
The review gives molecular-weight ranges of 26 to 37 kDa for stem bromelain and 24.5 to 32 kDa for fruit bromelain.
Reported optimal conditions differ by extract: stem bromelain pH 6 to 7 and 50 to 60 C, fruit bromelain pH 3 to 8 and 37 to 70 C.
Animal experiments summarized by the review reported very low bromelain toxicity, with a lethal dose greater than 10 g/kg body weight.
The review reports that dogs and rats treated with bromelain did not show cytotoxic or carcinogenic effects in the cited experiments.
The review notes that long-term bromelain administration may cause tachycardia in people with hypertension.
The authors report unpublished HUVEC data in which bromelain did not reduce endothelial-cell survival at concentrations up to 50 ug/mL.
The review estimates that about 40% of functionally intact bromelain may be present in rat blood after oral administration, with the highest concentration within one hour.

atoms.canonical_statement: Castell et al., as summarized by the review, reported a bromelain half-life of 6 to 9 hours.
The review warns that bromelain can provoke IgE-mediated respiratory allergy, especially in people allergic to pineapple.
The review reports anticoagulant and fibrinolytic actions of bromelain, including thrombus disruption, reduced platelet clumping, and reduced blood viscosity.
In a cited series of 73 patients with acute thrombophlebitis, bromelain combined with painkillers was associated with reduced pain, swelling, and fever.

exposures.details: Combined with painkillers; regimen not reported in the review

concept.text: Inflammatory symptoms including pain, swelling, and high temperature

atoms.canonical_statement: In an isolated rat-heart ischemia-reperfusion model, bromelain treatment improved left-ventricular function during reperfusion and increased aortic flow compared with untreated hearts.
The review reports that bromelain decreases platelet aggregation in a dose-dependent manner in ex vivo, in vitro, and in vivo studies.
A cited study reported concentration-dependent dual coagulation effects, procoagulant at low bromelain concentrations and anticoagulant at high concentrations.
At high concentrations, bromelain was reported to inhibit prothrombin-to-thrombin conversion, prolong PT and APTT, and reduce ADP-induced platelet aggregation.
The review reports that bromelain promotes conversion of plasminogen to plasmin and increases fibrin degradation.
The review reports dose-dependent decreases in PGE2 and thromboxane A2 activity, shifting the thromboxane A2 to prostacyclin ratio toward prostacyclin.
In animal diarrhea models, bromelain supplementation was reported to reduce bacterial toxin secretion by 35% to 62%, depending on the microorganism.
The review reports greater effectiveness when bromelain was combined with antibiotics than when antibiotics were used alone across several infection syndromes.
Rat experiments summarized by the review found increased penicillin and gentamicin concentrations when bromelain was coadministered.
Human studies summarized by the review reported higher blood or tissue concentrations of tetracycline and amoxicillin during bromelain administration.
A pediatric sepsis study summarized by the review reported early improvement when bromelain, rutin, and trypsin were used with antibiotics.
In chronic bacterial prostatitis, a combination containing bromelain was reported to improve levofloxacin clinical efficacy and quality of life, with no side effects observed during therapy.
Bromelain-capped gold nanoparticles carrying levofloxacin showed greater in vitro antibacterial activity against E. coli and S. aureus than levofloxacin alone.
The review reports anthelmintic activity against gastrointestinal nematodes, attributed to proteolytic damage of structural proteins in the nematode cuticle.
The review notes that bromelain anthelmintic activity is weaker in vivo than in vitro, potentially because of the acidic digestive environment and intestinal microbial and protozoal fauna.
The review reports antifungal activity, including fungicidal activity of bromelain plus trypsin against Candida albicans and activity against several Fusarium species.
The review reports antibacterial activity against oral pathogens including Enterococcus faecalis, Streptococcus mutans, Streptococcus sanguis, and Staphylococcus aureus.
Across LPS-stimulated cell models, bromelain was reported to suppress IL-6, IL-1beta, and TNF-alpha and inhibit NF-kappaB and MAPK signaling.
Bromelain was reported to inhibit inducible nitric oxide synthase expression in a dose-dependent manner in LPS-related models.
In IL-10-deficient mice with established colitis, oral bromelain was reported to reduce the incidence and severity of spontaneous colitis and colonic inflammation.
In human colonic biopsy organ cultures from ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, bromelain was reported to reduce secretion of several inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
The review reports proteolytic degradation of leukocyte surface molecules involved in migration, adhesion, and activation, including CD44, CD45R, CD62L, and CD8.

The review describes context-dependent immunomodulation: bromelain can increase inflammatory mediators in resting immune cells but suppress cytokine production in already activated inflammatory cells.
The review reports that bromelain can increase T-cell proliferation and costimulatory activity in immune-system models.

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 organizes anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory evidence by target model, experimental approach, molecular effect, and cited source.
The review states that existing clinical trials of bromelain in cancer provide little information on antitumor activity.
Figure 1 depicts three proposed anticancer routes for bromelain: modulation of signaling and gene expression, induction of apoptosis or autophagy, and cell-cycle arrest.
Breast-cancer studies summarized by the review report reduced proliferation and colony formation, apoptosis activation, and G2/M cell-cycle inhibition after bromelain exposure.
Melanoma and epidermoid-carcinoma studies summarized by the review report increased apoptosis-related signaling and reduced NF-kappaB, COX-2, Akt, and ERK pathway activity after bromelain treatment.
The review summarizes bromelain-associated programmed cell death in chronic myelogenous leukemia and lymphoma models.

atoms.canonical_statement: Gastrointestinal and colorectal cancer models in the review show apoptosis, cell-cycle effects, autophagy, and, in one KRASG12D model, ferroptosis-related effects after bromelain exposure.
The review reports antiproliferative and pro-apoptotic effects of bromelain in hepatic and pancreatic cancer models.
The review describes bromelain-associated autophagy, including increased LC3BII and beclin 1 in several cancer-cell models.

The review reports chemosensitizing effects when bromelain is combined with agents such as N-acetylcysteine, gemcitabine, fluorouracil, oxaliplatin, doxorubicin, or cisplatin in preclinical cancer models.
The review reports that bromelain can raise reactive oxygen species in some immune and cancer-cell models, with downstream oxidative stress, cell-cycle arrest, autophagy, or apoptosis.

Table 2 compiles cancer models, bromelain treatment approaches, molecular effects, and cited sources across breast, melanoma, leukemia, gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, pancreatic, sarcoma, and oral-cancer systems.
Postoperative otorhinolaryngology reports summarized by the review describe reduced edema, pain, swelling, and inflammatory signs with bromelain.
The review describes bromelain-based enzymatic debridement as effective for removing damaged extracellular-matrix components and eschar.
The review notes low selectivity of bromelain-based NexoBrid enzymatic debridement and toxic effects on viable human skin cells, especially at high concentrations.
The review reports improved efficacy for degenerative joint pain when bromelain is used in combination with agents such as diclofenac, rutin, trypsin, or turmeric.
Human exercise studies summarized by the review report that protease mixtures containing bromelain can reduce post-exercise muscle-strength loss and support faster recovery.
In VeroE6-cell experiments summarized by the review, bromelain reduced ACE2 and TMPRSS2 expression and cleaved both host-cell ACE2 and SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 2 proposes that bromelain could affect SARS-CoV-2 entry, inflammatory signaling, coagulation and fibrinolysis, platelet aggregation, and the bradykinin system.
The review proposes bromelain as a possible complementary therapy for COVID-19 and post-COVID-19 because of antiviral, anti-inflammatory, anticoagulant, and other biological actions.

source_anchor.paragraph: Section 9.2 Possible Management of Bromelain in COVID-19

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that bromelain's apparent anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity had not been tested in vivo in animal or human models.

The authors conclude that bromelain shows promise across cardiovascular, coagulation and fibrinolysis, infectious, inflammatory, and cancer applications, while its mechanism of action remains incompletely understood.
The authors describe bromelain as a possible oral enzyme-therapy candidate because it is absorbed after oral administration and the reviewed literature reports few significant side effects.
The review identifies bromelain instability under high acidity, gastric proteases, chemicals, organic solvents, and elevated temperature as a barrier to practical use.
The authors call for more work on bromelain mechanisms, purification, stabilization, and lower-cost production before broad application.
